questions.q: Why did Meridian Parts' assumption that its inbound endpoint URL was safe because it 'wasn't published anywhere' fail?
options: Because Salesforce Site URLs are discoverable regardless of whether they're published -- an unpublished URL is not the same as a secret, and relying on that alone is security through obscurity
Because Salesforce Sites cannot host inbound Apex REST endpoints at all
Because the researcher was a Meridian employee with insider access
Because the endpoint had signature verification that was misconfigured
questions.explain: The case study explicitly frames this as security through obscurity: an unpublished but technically discoverable URL is not a real control, which is exactly why signature verification (not secrecy of the URL) is the standard fix.

questions.q: What made the inbound endpoint's data exposure broader than just the junk Order records the researcher created?
options: Order records automatically cascade access to related Account records regardless of profile
The researcher also compromised the System Administrator password directly
The endpoint had no relationship to any guest user profile
The guest user profile behind the Site had read/write access to Account and Contact as well, because it was cloned from an existing profile instead of scoped from scratch
questions.explain: Cloning an existing, broader profile instead of scoping the guest user profile to exactly what the endpoint needed meant the endpoint's blast radius extended into Account and Contact data that had nothing to do with its actual job.

questions.q: Which combination of gaps does this lesson identify in Meridian's outbound integration credential specifically?
options: A correctly-scoped Named Credential using JWT Bearer flow, with only a minor IP-range gap
No OAuth flow was used at all -- the integration had no authentication whatsoever

The wrong OAuth flow for an unattended integration, a credential typed directly into a config screen instead of using Named Credentials, and an identity with far more access (System Administrator) than needed
A Per-User principal that was never approved by any individual user
questions.explain: The outbound side combined three separate gaps at once: Username-Password flow (wrong choice for an unattended integration), the password hardcoded into the middleware tool's config, and a System Administrator-level identity far beyond what the integration needed.

questions.q: This lesson distinguishes 'root cause' from 'detection gap' in a post-incident review. Which statement correctly reflects that distinction as applied to Meridian?
options: Detection gaps only matter if no root cause can be identified
Fixing the root cause automatically fixes the detection gap, so only one needs to be addressed

The missing signature verification and over-broad guest profile are root causes; a security review on any reasonable cadence, or an accountable owner's periodic check, is what would have caught these sooner -- a separate, detection-focused fix
Root cause and detection gap are the same thing, just described with different words
questions.explain: Root cause is the underlying design gap that created the exposure; detection gap is the separate, missing ability to have noticed it sooner even without the design fix -- a thorough remediation plan addresses both, since a future different problem still needs to be caught quickly.

questions.q: What role did the lack of a named owner and monitoring play in the Meridian Parts incident, per this lesson?
options: The contractor who built the integration remained its owner for the full three years

Nobody was accountable for noticing any of these gaps over three years, and no baseline or alerting existed that would have flagged unusual activity sooner, even independent of the design flaws themselves
Monitoring was in place but simply wasn't reviewed
None -- ownership and monitoring are unrelated to this incident
questions.explain: No owner was named after the contractor left, and no monitoring or periodic review was ever established -- which meant the three-year-unrotated credential and the exposed endpoint both had no one positioned to notice them sooner.
